source_refs.note: Book p. 15: 1.6 definition, inverse of exponential, common/natural log, basic identities (4th misprinted), laws and change of base

blocks.text: A logarithmic function is defined by \(y = \log_a x\), \(a > 0\), \(a \ne 1\), \(x > 0\). It assigns to each positive real number \(x\) a unique real number \(y\), such that \(a^{y} = x\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A logarithm answers one question: to what power must the base \(a\) be raised to give \(x\)? For example \(\log_2 8 = 3\) because \(2^{3} = 8\), and \(\log_3 \frac{1}{9} = -2\) because \(3^{-2} = \frac{1}{9}\).
Why the conditions? \(a > 0\) keeps every power \(a^{y}\) defined for all real \(y\); \(a \ne 1\) is needed because \(1^{y} = 1\) always, so base 1 could never produce any other number; and \(x > 0\) because a positive base raised to any power is always positive, so a logarithm of zero or of a negative number does not exist.
Logarithmic Function as Inverse of Exponential Function

We know that the exponential function
\[y = a^{x},\ (a > 0,\ a \ne 1)\]
is a one-to-one function with domain \(]-\infty, \infty[\) and range \(]0, \infty[\). Thus, it is invertible. Interchanging \(x\) and \(y\), we obtain:
\[x = a^{y}\]
\[\Rightarrow y = \log_a x\]
Hence, the logarithmic function is the inverse of the exponential function with domain \(]0, \infty[\) and range \(]-\infty, \infty[\).

blocks.caption: Teaching note: our comparison of the two functions (not printed in the book)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Interchanging \(x\) and \(y\) is exactly what an inverse does: the inputs of one function are the outputs of the other. That is why the domain and range simply swap places, and why every point \((p, q)\) of \(y = a^{x}\) becomes the point \((q, p)\) of \(y = \log_a x\). In 1.8 you will see this as a reflection in the line \(y = x\).

A logarithm with base 10 is called a common logarithm and a logarithm with base \(e\) is called a natural logarithm and we write:
\[\log_{10} b = \log b\]
\[\log_e b = \ln b\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: \(e \approx 2.71828\) is the special number you met with \(y = e^{x}\) in 1.4. On a calculator the key \(\log\) gives the common logarithm and the key \(\ln\) gives the natural logarithm. When no base is written, \(\log\) means base 10 in this book.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the fourth identity as \(\log_a x = x\). That is false: for example \(\log_2 8 = 3\), not 8. The correct identity is \(a^{\log_a x} = x\) for \(x > 0\): raising the base to the logarithm of \(x\) gives \(x\) back.

blocks.title: Teaching note

blocks.text: Laws of Logarithms and Change of Base Formula
For \(a > 0\), \(a \ne 1\), \(x > 0\), \(y > 0\), \(t \in \mathbb{R}\), we have studied the following laws of logarithms and change of base formula:

items: Change of Base Formula: \(\log_a x = \frac{\log_b x}{\log_b a}\) for every \(b > 0\), \(b \ne 1\). In particular:

blocks.text_alt: log of x to the base a equals ln x over ln a
log of x to the base a equals log x over log a, with common logarithms

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why the laws hold: they are the laws of exponents in disguise. If \(x = a^{m}\) and \(y = a^{n}\), then \(xy = a^{m+n}\), so \(\log_a(xy) = m + n = \log_a x + \log_a y\). In the same way \(\frac{x}{y} = a^{m-n}\) gives the quotient law and \(x^{t} = a^{tm}\) gives the power law.
Why the change of base formula is useful: a calculator has only \(\log\) (base 10) and \(\ln\) (base \(e\)). To find \(\log_2 5\) we write \(\log_2 5 = \frac{\ln 5}{\ln 2} \approx \frac{1.6094}{0.6931} \approx 2.3219\) (our example). Check: \(2^{2.3219} \approx 5\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(y = \log_a x\) means \(a^{y} = x\), with \(a > 0\), \(a \ne 1\), \(x > 0\).
2. \(\log_a x\) is the inverse of \(a^{x}\): domain \(]0, \infty[\), range \(]-\infty, \infty[\).
3. \(\log b\) means \(\log_{10} b\) and \(\ln b\) means \(\log_e b\).
4. \(\log_a 1 = 0\), \(\log_a a = 1\), \(\log_a(a^{x}) = x\), \(a^{\log_a x} = x\).
5. Product, quotient and power laws; change of base \(\log_a x = \frac{\ln x}{\ln a}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\log_a(x + y) = \log_a x + \log_a y\). The product law is about \(xy\), not \(x + y\).
2. Writing \(\frac{\log_a x}{\log_a y} = \log_a \frac{x}{y}\). The quotient law is about \(\log_a \frac{x}{y} = \log_a x - \log_a y\).
3. Taking the logarithm of 0 or of a negative number: \(\log_a x\) needs \(x > 0\).
4. Copying the misprinted identity \(\log_a x = x\); the true one is \(a^{\log_a x} = x\).
